Makki according to all.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾, has three interpretations:

One: tabaraka is a form (tafa'ul) derived from barakah (blessing). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

It is more emphatic than mubarak, because blessedness belongs exclusively to God, while being blessed is shared by created beings.

The second: i.e., He blessed in creation by what He placed in them of blessing. This is said by Ibn 'Ata'.

The third: its meaning is "He exalted and rose high." This is said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Regarding His saying, ﴿in whose hand is the dominion﴾, there are two interpretations:

One: the dominion of the heavens and the earth, in this world and the Hereafter.

The second: the dominion of prophethood, through which He honoured those who follow Him and humbled those who oppose Him. This is said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾, whether in bestowal or in retribution.

﴿He who created death and life﴾, meaning death in this world and life in the Hereafter.

Qatadah said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "God humbled the children of Adam through death, and made this world a house of life and then a house of death, and made the Hereafter a house of recompense and then a house of permanence."

The second: He created death and life as two bodies. He created death in the form of a white-spotted ram, and He created life in the form of a mare [a white-spotted female]. This is a transmitted report related by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

﴿That He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations: One: which of you is most complete in intellect. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: which of you is most ascetic toward this world. This is said by Sufyan.

The third: which of you is most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God and quickest to obey God. This is a transmitted view.

The fourth: which of you remembers death most, prepares for it best, and fears and beware of it most. This is said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: which of you knows the faults of his own self best.

It may also admit a sixth: which of you is most content with His decree and most patient under His trial.

﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: i.e., harmonious and similar, derived from the saying, "This is muṭābiq to that," i.e., similar to it. This is said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: meaning some of them above others. al-Hasan said: and the seven earths are above one another, and between every heaven and earth there is creation and command.

﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

One: from disparity, said by Qatadah, and from it is the poet's saying:
"Disparate [mounts] from the reins, bent [in pace], until, at evening, of their burdens..."

The second: from defect, said by al-Suddi.

The third: from dispersal, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that one part does not outpace another, said by 'Ata' ibn Abi Muslim.

The poet said:
"I shall not overtake what has passed from me, by lament, nor by 'if only' and 'had I but'."

﴿Then return the vision﴾. Qatadah said: its meaning is, look toward the sky.

﴿Do you see any breaks?﴾ Regarding this there are four interpretations:

One: cracks, said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The second: gaps, said by Qatadah.

The third: holes, said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: weakness, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Then return the vision twice﴾, i.e., look at the sky once after another.

His command to look twice may admit two interpretations:

One: because in the second look the sight is stronger and the vision sharper.

The second: because in the second look he sees, in the movement of its stars and the variation of its constellations, what he did not see the first time, so he ascertains that there is no break in it.

Some have interpreted with a third aspect: that by the "two times" is meant the heart and the sight.

﴿Your vision will return to you dazzled while it is fatigued﴾, i.e., the vision returns to you because it sees no breaks, so it recoils.

Regarding "dazzled" (khasi'an) there are four interpretations:

One: humiliated, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: cut off, said by al-Suddi.

The third: weary, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The fourth: distanced, said by al-Akhfash, derived from "khasa'ta al-kalb" when you drive the dog away.

Regarding "fatigued" (ḥasīr) there are three interpretations:

One: that it means regretful, and from it is the poet's saying:
"I am not today upon anything that has passed, O daughter of the smith, who turned back in regret."

The second: that it means weary, which has weakened from perceiving its object, said by Ibn 'Abbas, and from it is the poet's saying:
"Whoever extends his gaze beyond its limit, his sight returns dazzled and exhausted."

The third: that it means cut off from fatigue, said by al-Suddi, and from it is the poet's saying:
"And the horses are dusty, their steeds still, exhausted, leaving their foals behind on the road."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 67, verses 6–11:**

﴿When they are cast into it﴾: meaning the disbelievers are cast into Jahannam (Hell).(p-53)

﴿They will hear from it a roaring (shahīq)﴾: concerning this there are two opinions:

One: that the shahīq (roaring, groaning intake of breath) comes from the disbelievers when they are cast into the Fire.

The second: that the shahīq belongs to Jahannam when the disbelievers are cast into it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It breathes toward them with a shahqah (a loud gasp) like the gasp of a mule for barley, then it exhales a zafrah (a roaring exhalation), and no one remains who does not fear."

Regarding the shahīq there are three views:

One: that the shahīq is in the chests, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second: that it is the shouting, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: that the shahīq is the final bray of the donkey, and the zafīr is like the first bray of the donkey. It was also said that the zafīr comes from the throat and the shahīq from the chest.

﴿And it boils (taf'ur)﴾: meaning it seethes (taghlī). From this is the poet's saying:

"You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, while the people's pot is hot and boiling."

﴿It nearly bursts apart from fury (tamayyazu min al-ghayz)﴾: concerning this there are two views:

One: it is cut apart, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: it separates, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

As for His saying (min al-ghayz) here, there are two views:

One: that it is the boiling (ghalayān), as the poet said:

"O heart, be patient, though it is angry and has boiled up with fury in the midst of the people, so that it does not strike you."

The second: that it is anger (ghadab), meaning wrath against the people of disobedience and vengeance by Allah upon them.

﴿Did there not come to you a warner?﴾: concerning this there are two views:

One: that the warners (nudhur) are from the jinn and the messengers from mankind, as said by Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 67, verses 12–15:

﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ Regarding this, there are six opinions:

First: "The unseen" (al-ghayb) is Allah the Exalted and His angels. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

Second: It is Paradise and Hellfire. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: It is the Qur'an. This was said by Zirr ibn Hubaysh.

Fourth: It is Islam, because it is hidden (yaghib). This was said by Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid.

Fifth: It is the heart. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Sixth: It is solitude: when a person is alone with himself and recalls his sin, he seeks forgiveness from his Lord. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿For them is forgiveness﴾ Regarding this, there are three opinions:

First: Through repentance and seeking forgiveness.

Second: Through their fear of their Lord unseen.

Third: Because by avoiding sins they have come to occupy the station of one who has been forgiven.

﴿And a great reward﴾ means Paradise.

It may also bear another meaning: that it is pardon from punishment and the multiplication of reward.

﴿It is He who made the earth subservient to you﴾ meaning made tame and easy.

Qatadah related from Abu al-Jald that the earth is twenty-four thousand farsakh: for the Sudan are twelve [thousand], for the Romans [eight thousand], for the Persians three thousand, and for the Arabs one thousand.

﴿So walk through its slopes﴾ Regarding this, there are three opinions:

First: In its mountains. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Bashir ibn Ka'b.

Second: In its far regions and its wide roads. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. (p-55)

Third: In its regions.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: in the places where its crops and trees grow. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿and eat of His provision﴾ Regarding this, there are two opinions:

First: Of what He has made lawful for you. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: Of what He has made grow for you. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾ meaning the raising (al-ba'th).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 67, verses 20–27:

﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ This is a parable (*mathal*) that Allah struck for guidance and misguidance. Its meaning is: not the one who walks prone on his face, unable to see ahead of him, to his right, or to his left, [is the same as]

one who walks upright, balanced, looking at what is before him, to his right, and to his left. On this there are two views:

The first: It is a parable Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever. The one prone on his face is the disbeliever, who stumbles headlong in his disbelief, while the one who walks upright is the believer, who is guided by his faith. The meaning is: "Is the one who walks in error better guided, or the one who walks rightly guided?" This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: The one prone on his face is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and the one who walks upright is 'Ammar ibn Yasir. This was said by 'Ikrima.

﴿on a straight path﴾. On this there are two views:

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 67, verse 28–30:

﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken into the earth, then who will bring you flowing water?﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

﴿Then who will bring you clear water?﴾ Concerning this there are four views:

The first: that its meaning is "sweet." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is "pure." This was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

The third: that it is that which is fed by springs so that it never ceases.

The fourth: that it is "flowing." This was said by Qatada, and from it is the verse of Jarir:

"Indeed those who departed with your heart left behind a trickle in your eye that never ceases to flow."
